questions.q: They didn't read me my rights. Can you get my case dismissed?
questions.a: This is the most common question we get. Unfortunately, the answer is usually no. It is only required that your rights be read to you when you are questioned by the police after being arrested. In a DWI situation, the arrest usually occurs after you have already performed the field sobriety tests and answered questions about where you have been and what you have been drinking.

questions.q: Can a DWI be sealed or expunged after deferred adjudication?
questions.a: Deferred adjudication is not available in DWIs, so even a probation for DWI is considered a conviction and cannot be sealed or expunged.

questions.q: The police are on the phone. What do I do?
questions.a: First, calm down. Are you a witness or a suspect? If you may be a suspect, you really need to speak with a criminal attorney before speaking to the police at all. Do not lie to the police; it is okay not to speak to them at all. A police officer has no authority to promise you anything, and the only person who can make a deal with you is the prosecuting attorney.

questions.q: So, what is deferred adjudication in a family violence case?
questions.a: Deferred adjudication is a type of probation: you enter a plea of guilty, but the judge does not find you guilty, your punishment is not assessed, and you are placed directly on probation. In family violence and sex cases, however, you might as well be convicted, as the consequences are about the same, and the records cannot be sealed afterwards.

questions.q: Does a family violence case affect my firearms?
questions.a: Any family violence case, even when deferred, will bar you from ever possessing or owning a firearm.

services.title: Expunction
services.text: Petitions to erase the record of an arrest where the case was dismissed outright or ended in an acquittal.
services.lead: Getting an expunction granted erases the existence of an arrest. The fingerprints and mugshots are destroyed, and all references to the arrest and charges are deleted from the various government computers.

covers.title: Who is eligible
covers.text: To be eligible for an expunction the case must have been outright dismissed, meaning no probation and no deferred adjudication were completed. If it was a felony case that was indicted, there are more limitations and exclusions.

covers.title: Waiting for the limitations period
covers.text: In many cases you have to wait several years for the statute of limitations to run out before you can petition the court to have the records expunged.

covers.title: After an acquittal
covers.text: If you get an acquittal at trial, you can ask for an automatic short-form expunction.

covers.title: Old cases are worth a look
covers.text: Even dismissed charges sometimes come back to haunt you when looking for a job or housing, or if you get into trouble again in the future.

covers.title: One caveat
covers.text: Once an expunction is granted it is as though the arrest never happened, except for an issue of whether the federal government recognizes a state expunction order.

questions.q: What is the difference between expunction and nondisclosure?
questions.a: An expunction erases the existence of an arrest, and the defendant can deny ever being arrested, with a very limited exception for testifying under oath. A nondisclosure does not erase an arrest or the records relating to the probation, but it does substantially limit the general public, including landlords and employers, from accessing the information.

services.title: Nondisclosure
services.text: Orders sealing the records of a successfully completed deferred adjudication from landlords, employers and the general public.
services.lead: You can ask for a nondisclosure order after successfully completing a deferred adjudication in most cases, which will effectively seal the records from the public while still keeping the information available to law enforcement and governmental agencies. Our office can handle a request for a nondisclosure order at the appropriate time.

covers.title: Waiting periods
covers.text: Some misdemeanors are immediately eligible on completion of deferred adjudication probation. All eligible felony offenses require a five-year wait from the end of probation, and a listed group of misdemeanors requires a two-year wait.

covers.title: Staying clean during the wait
covers.text: During the two- and five-year wait, if applicable, you may not have any convictions or deferred adjudications for anything other than a fine-only traffic offense.

covers.title: Offences that cannot be sealed
covers.text: Family violence cases, any registerable sex offense, aggravated kidnapping, murder, injury to a child or elderly person, child endangerment or abandonment, violation of a protective order, and stalking. If you have ever been convicted of or received a deferred adjudication for any of those offenses, you may not have any offense sealed.

covers.title: The judge decides
covers.text: Nondisclosures are at the discretion of the judge who granted the probation.

covers.title: The misdemeanors that wait two years
covers.text: Unlawful restraint, public lewdness or indecent exposure, abuse of 911, deadly conduct, terroristic threat, cruelty to animals, all weapons cases, riot, enticing a child or harboring a runaway, false alarm, assault other than family violence, disrupting a meeting, harassment, abuse of a corpse, bigamy, bomb cases, Class B disorderly conduct and obstructing a highway.

The fact that you have been charged, entered a plea and been placed on probation will be in the public records. You may have the option to have the records sealed, not expunged, after successfully completing the probation, depending on your record and the offense.

questions.q: Does a family violence case affect my firearms?
questions.a: Any family violence case, even when deferred, will bar you from ever possessing or owning a firearm.

about.title: We are a family, and we will treat you like family as well.
text: Turner Garrison Law is a criminal defense law firm located in Baytown, Texas. Our firm has successfully represented clients accused of or under investigation for an array of criminal charges, and we have over 60 years of combined experience.

We handle a variety of cases, including DWI/DUI defense, in Harris County, Liberty County, Chambers County, and other counties across the Houston metropolitan area. We have tried approximately 200 jury trials in cases ranging from DWI and drug possession to murder and child sexual assaults.

We strongly believe in your right to legal representation. We know that an arrest or a criminal charge may have a substantial impact on your future. The uncertainty of the situation is scary and confusing; the jargon often difficult to understand. An experienced and knowledgeable attorney can walk you through each step and guide you to the best outcome. You have rights; let us protect those rights for you.

faqs.q: My lawyer said I wouldn't have a record if I took a deferred adjudication, but it still shows up. What gives?
faqs.a: Deferred adjudication is a form of probation, which in most situations is not considered a conviction. That does not mean that you have no record. The fact that you have been charged, entered a plea and been placed on probation will be in the public records. You may have the option to have the records sealed, not expunged, after successfully completing the probation, depending on your record and the offense. Deferred adjudication is not available in DWIs, so even a probation for DWI is considered a conviction and cannot be sealed or expunged. Our office can handle a request for a nondisclosure order at the appropriate time.

faqs.q: What is the difference between expunction and nondisclosure?
faqs.a: Getting an expunction granted erases the existence of an arrest. The fingerprints and mugshots are destroyed and all references to the arrest and charges are deleted from the various government computers. To be eligible, the case must have been outright dismissed, meaning no probation and no deferred adjudication were completed. Nondisclosure is a different matter. It gives a person who has successfully completed a deferred adjudication, with many exceptions including family violence and sex crimes, the ability to have the records sealed from disclosure to non-governmental entities. A nondisclosure order does not erase an arrest, but it does substantially limit the general public, including landlords and employers, from accessing the information.

faqs.q: The police are on the phone. What do I do?
faqs.a: First, calm down. Are you a witness or a suspect? If you are really just a witness and plan on telling them the truth, go for it. If you may be a suspect, you really need to speak with a criminal attorney before speaking to the police at all. Do not lie to the police; it is okay not to speak to them at all, but if you lie you are getting yourself into a much bigger problem. The police will treat you differently if you go in without an attorney: they will imply that you do not need one, that you must be guilty if you want to speak to one, and that things will go easier on you if you just talk to them. A police officer has absolutely no authority to promise you anything; the only person who can make a deal with you is the prosecuting attorney, who is likely not even involved at this point. If it is in fact in your best interest to admit to some wrongdoing and assist with the investigation, please wait and let an attorney make that determination and try to get you something in return for your cooperation. There is a reason you have the right to remain silent.

faqs.q: They didn't read me my rights. Can you get my case dismissed?
faqs.a: This is the most common question we get. Unfortunately, the answer is usually no. It is only required that your rights be read to you when you are questioned by the police after being arrested. In a DWI situation, the arrest usually occurs after you have already performed the field sobriety tests and answered questions about where you have been and what you have been drinking. In most other situations you will not be questioned after arrest, so it is not necessary that your Miranda rights be read to you.

faqs.q: So, what is deferred adjudication, anyway?
faqs.a: Deferred adjudication is a type of probation. With regular probation you are found guilty and put on probation, so your record will show a conviction. When you take a deferred adjudication, essentially you are entering a plea of guilty, but the judge does not find you guilty, your punishment is not assessed, and you are placed directly on probation. The main benefit is that if you successfully complete your probation then you will not have a conviction for the offense. In family violence and sex cases, however, you might as well be convicted, as the consequences are about the same. The big risk is that if you violate this type of probation and the judge revokes your deferred adjudication, he or she can sentence you up to the maximum penalty available for the crime you pled to, and generally you cannot appeal that decision. If someone looked up your record after a successfully completed deferred adjudication, it would show that you were arrested and successfully completed it.
